title: Quorum
explain: A quorum is the minimum number of votes that lets a group decide. For agreement, the quorum is a majority: floor(N/2) + 1 of N nodes. The whole trick is arithmetic: any two majorities of the same group overlap in at least one node, so two conflicting decisions cannot both succeed.
model:
My analogy is a jury: a verdict needs a majority, and two different verdicts cannot both have one.

```
5 nodes, quorum = 3
side 1 {A,B,C}  3 votes ✓ can decide
side 2 {D,E}    2 votes ✗ must wait         (any two majorities share a node)
```

- **Intersection property:** two sets of size > N/2 cannot be disjoint. The shared node saw both decisions, so conflicts are caught.
- **Network split:** at most one side holds a majority.
- **Fault tolerance:** f = floor((N−1)/2) failures, N = 2f + 1: 3 tolerates 1, 5 tolerates 2, 7 tolerates 3.
- **Even sizes waste a node:** 4 need 3 votes and still tolerate 1, and a 2/2 split leaves nobody a majority.
- **Failure domains:** 3 nodes in one datacenter and 2 in another means losing the big one halts the cluster.

Two flavours share the idea: majority quorums for *agreement* ([consensus](#/sd/f/consensus), [Raft](#/sd/f/raft), leader election) and tunable `W + R > N` quorums for *replicated data* ([leaderless quorum](#/sd/f/leaderless-quorum), [quorum-based replication](#/sd/f/quorum-based-replication)). The price: without enough live nodes, the group refuses to answer.

details.q: How many votes make a quorum in a 7-node cluster?
details.a: Four: floor(7/2) + 1. It tolerates three failures.

details.q: I need to keep deciding through three simultaneous failures. How big a cluster?
Why is a 4-node cluster no better than 3?
details.a: Both tolerate one failure (4 need 3 votes). The extra node adds cost and a 2/2 split in which no side has a majority.

details.q: Five nodes are split 3 and 2 and a client writes to each side. What happens?
details.a: The 3-node side commits; the 2-node side refuses the write. Only one side can hold a majority, so there is no split brain.

details.q: A 5-node cluster has 3 nodes in datacenter A and 2 in B. Which failure stops decisions?
details.a: Losing datacenter A: only 2 nodes remain, below the majority of 3. Losing B leaves 3 and still works. Spread nodes so no single domain holds a majority, or accept that domain as a single point of failure.
Availability when too many nodes are unreachable (it refuses rather than answers wrongly) and a round trip to the majority per decision.

prompts.q: State the quorum intersection property and say what it prevents.
points: Any two majorities share at least one node
Two conflicting decisions cannot both be accepted
Prevents split brain across a partition

prompts.q: Size a cluster for two simultaneous failures and place its nodes.
points: Spread over failure domains so no domain has a majority
Accept refusal when the quorum is lost

prompts.q: Explain the two flavours of quorum and how they differ.
points: W + R > N for replicated data
Tunable is available but only mostly fresh
